title: The 10,000-hour rule: Ericsson's violin study, deliberate practice and later meta-analyses

sources.title: Deliberate Practice and Proposed Limits on the Effects of Practice on the Acquisition of Expert Performance: Why the Original Definition Matters and Recommendations for Future Research

sources.publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine (PubMed Central); Macnamara & Maitra, Royal Society Open Science (2019)
sources.title: The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer (1993)
The 10,000 Hour Rule Is Not Real (2014)
sources.note: 只取 2014 年整合分析的研究篇數；此文引述其他媒體的內容一律不取

sources.title: Practice Will Make You Better, but Maybe Not the Best (2019)

facts.text: Malcolm Gladwell popularized the 10,000-hour rule in his 2008 book Outliers, presenting about 10,000 hours of practice as the key to expert skill and citing Ericsson's 1993 study as his main evidence.
In 1993 Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer studied three groups of 10 violin students at the Music Academy of West Berlin: the best, the good, and future music teachers.
By age 18, the best students in the 1993 study had practiced alone for about 7,410 hours on average, the good students about 5,301 hours, and the future music teachers about 3,420 hours.

Derived from f3: by age 18 the best group had about 2,109 (roughly 2,100) more hours of solo practice than the good group and about 3,990 (roughly 4,000) more hours than the future teachers; the good group's 5,301 hours is roughly 5,300.
Ericsson said his research showed that long practice was needed but found no magic number of hours; he estimated that winners of international piano competitions practice about 25,000 hours.
Ericsson defined deliberate practice as practice designed by a skilled teacher, with a clear goal, immediate feedback on each attempt, and repeated attempts that are gradually improved.
Gladwell wrote about practice in general and did not use the term deliberate practice.
In 2014 Brooke Macnamara and colleagues combined the results of 88 studies on practice and performance.

The 2014 meta-analysis found that deliberate practice explained 26 percent of the differences in performance in games, 21 percent in music, 18 percent in sports, 4 percent in education and less than 1 percent in professions.

Ericsson and Harwell reanalyzed the 2014 data, keeping only studies that met their stricter criteria; practice then explained 29 percent of the differences, or 61 percent after correcting for measurement error.
In 2019 Macnamara and Maitra repeated the violin study with 39 violinists; the best and the good violinists did not differ significantly in how much they had practiced alone.
In the 2019 replication, practice alone explained about 26 percent of the differences in performance, compared with 48 percent reported in the original study.
Other researchers have found that working memory can help explain differences in musicians' abilities, and talent and genes are also thought to play a part.

notes: Guardian 的內容（含其他媒體轉引的部分）一律不取；2014 年整合分析的「整體解釋量」各來源寫 12% 或 14%，說法不一，文章不寫
